# Global AI Investment and Delivery by Major International Consulting Firms, 2023–September 2026

The major consulting and professional-services firms have moved from isolated generative-AI experiments toward enterprise platforms, industry agents, managed services, governance systems and workforce transformation. Accenture and Deloitte disclose the clearest large-scale commitments—about US$3 billion each on different scopes and horizons—while EY, PwC, KPMG and Capgemini report substantial commitments or AI-related spending whose definitions differ. IBM reports a US$12.5 billion generative-AI book of business rather than an AI-investment total, and the MBB firms generally disclose capability scale, alliances and client results instead of one headline investment figure.

The strongest delivered evidence is concentrated in specific deployments: Bain’s Bradesco chatbot, BCG’s banking and marketing cases, McKinsey’s pharmaceutical work, IBM’s CEMIG transformation, KPMG’s live enterprise platform and Accenture’s Sanofi program. At the same time, many headline figures remain announcements, bookings, pipeline counts, internal usage, survey findings or forward-looking targets. The firms increasingly converge on four commercial components—AI strategy, governed platforms, implementation or managed operations, and talent development—but differentiate themselves through scale, industry depth, technology alliances, governance, sovereignty and operating-model design.

## Roadmap and comparison rules

This report answers eight questions in sequence. It first identifies what each firm has actually disclosed about AI investment; then catalogs the major partnerships, acquisitions, centers and ecosystem programs. It next inventories named products and services, separates announced outputs from live or measured results, and examines client cases by problem, intervention and outcome. The final sections compare strategic directions and talent programs before bringing all ten firms together on common axes.

The comparison uses three distinctions throughout.

- An investment is a disclosed commitment, acquisition, research or capability-building expenditure. It is not interchangeable with bookings, revenue, backlog, platform access or a survey of client spending.
- An output is labeled as an announcement or target, development pipeline, pilot, live deployment, usage measure or measured business outcome.
- Evidence is strongest when a primary corporate or client case names the intervention and reports a result. Firm marketing pages, surveys and secondary comparisons remain useful, but their scope and methodology are stated rather than treated as independently validated proof.

Where the supplied evidence does not provide a requested amount, date, geography, product name or outcome, the field is marked “not disclosed,” “not stated” or “not retrieved.” That means the cited material does not establish the value; it does not prove that the activity does not exist.

## 1. Firm universe and global AI investment snapshot

The universe comprises Deloitte, PwC, EY and KPMG; Accenture; McKinsey, BCG and Bain; IBM; and Capgemini. IBM is included because its consulting, software, research and infrastructure businesses form an integrated AI proposition. Capgemini is included for the same reason: its consulting, engineering, operations and acquisitions are increasingly organized around enterprise AI delivery.

Accenture’s official material provides the clearest example of a global capability-building commitment. Its Singapore engineering hub was designed to extend the Center for Advanced AI, develop custom models and support applied research across healthcare, financial services, public-sector, energy and sustainability use cases. The hub also included local talent development in foundation models and responsible AI, showing that the commitment was intended to cover research, delivery and ecosystem formation rather than only software purchasing. [Accenture’s Singapore announcement](https://newsroom.accenture.com/news/2024/accenture-to-set-up-first-of-its-kind-ai-refinery-engineering-hub-in-singapore)

Deloitte’s disclosure is similarly large but differently defined. More than US$3 billion through FY2030 is earmarked for GenAI delivery and operations, products and offerings. Its geographic qualifier—more than 150 countries and territories—signals a global operating investment, but the announcement does not break the total into acquisitions, R&D, infrastructure, talent, products or client delivery.

EY illustrates why alliance spending and firm spending must be separated. The EY–Microsoft initiative is a confirmed joint investment of more than US$1 billion over five years, combining Microsoft engineers with EY professionals and change-management capabilities. A secondary comparison additionally describes a US$1.4 billion EY.ai investment program announced in 2023, but the supplied primary EY evidence does not confirm the amount or its exact accounting scope. The two figures should therefore not be added.

PwC’s reported US$1 billion commitment has the same limitation. The secondary benchmark describes it as a three-year PwC US forward commitment, not a global PwC investment. PwC’s official sources instead emphasize service categories, responsible-AI operating models, an AI studio and managed services. The strongest supported conclusion is that PwC has made a substantial AI capability commitment, but the supplied primary evidence does not support a like-for-like global dollar figure.

KPMG explicitly says Workbench forms part of the global organization’s multi-billion-dollar AI and agentic-transformation investment, while withholding the amount. A secondary account attributes a US$2 billion five-year Microsoft cloud-and-AI commitment and a US$12 billion new-revenue target to KPMG. Those figures are useful as reported market evidence, but the official KPMG material should control the ledger: the amount is undisclosed, and the revenue target is not a realized result.

For IBM, it would be misleading to treat total R&D or acquisitions as AI spending. IBM’s 2025 annual report says R&D expense was US$8.316 billion and that it was driven in part by AI, hybrid cloud and quantum innovation. IBM also completed US$9.346 billion of acquisitions, including HashiCorp, while describing the portfolio as advancing hybrid cloud and AI. Those figures demonstrate investment capacity and strategic direction, not a measured AI-only budget. [IBM’s 2025 Annual Report](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/51143/000005114326000010/ibm-20251231_d2.htm)

Capgemini’s official evidence has a similar boundary. The €3.8 billion acquisition total in 2025 notably includes WNS, which Capgemini says strengthens GenAI-powered intelligent operations and end-to-end agentification. It does not state WNS’s purchase price or the AI-related portion of the acquisition total. Capgemini’s separate €2 billion AI commitment remains a secondary-source figure in the supplied evidence.

### Why the amounts cannot be ranked directly

The figures differ along at least five dimensions:

1. **Time horizon.** Accenture, PwC, Capgemini and KPMG figures are described over different multi-year periods; Deloitte’s runs through FY2030; IBM’s R&D and acquisition figures are annual.
2. **Spend type.** Some figures are AI commitments, some are joint-alliance funding, some are acquisition totals, and some are broad R&D or capability-build costs.
3. **Geography.** PwC’s secondary figure is US-specific, while Accenture, Deloitte and Capgemini describe global programs. EY’s US$1 billion-plus initiative is global but jointly funded.
4. **Accounting boundary.** IBM’s R&D and Capgemini’s acquisition total span capabilities beyond AI.
5. **Status.** A commitment is not realized spend, and an alliance target is not revenue or deployment.

The strongest partial answer to the investment question is therefore not a single total. Accenture and Deloitte each disclose commitments above US$3 billion on broadly global scopes; EY and Microsoft disclose a joint global commitment above US$1 billion; KPMG discloses a multi-billion commitment without an amount; PwC and Capgemini have secondary three-year figures that lack equivalent primary confirmation; Bain, McKinsey, BCG and IBM do not disclose one comparable AI-only headline amount in the supplied evidence.

## 2. Key AI initiatives and ecosystems

The firms’ initiatives fall into four overlapping models:

- platform-led delivery, in which the firm packages models, data, agents and workflow tools;
- alliance-led delivery, in which a hyperscaler or model provider supplies core technology;
- operating-model and governance programs, in which the firm reshapes processes, controls and human roles;
- capability accumulation through acquisitions, research centers and talent ecosystems.

Accenture’s ecosystem is the most visibly industrialized of the consulting-led offerings. AI Refinery combines a branded platform, hyperscaler infrastructure, industry agents, regional engineering hubs and acquisitions. The logic is to shorten the path from a generic model to a domain workflow: for example, a clinical-trial companion, industrial asset troubleshooting or revenue-growth management. The announced reduction from months or weeks to days is a capability claim, not an independently measured average. [Accenture AI Refinery for Industry](https://newsroom.accenture.com/news/2025/accenture-launches-ai-refinery-for-industry-to-reinvent-processes-and-accelerate-agentic-ai-journeys)

Deloitte has built a more governance-conscious agentic ecosystem. The Global Agentic Network and Zora position autonomous agents as a connected product business, while Enterprise AI Navigator links use-case selection to financial impact, workflow redesign and technology readiness. Silicon2Service extends the proposition down into sovereign infrastructure and AI-factory management. The common thread is that Deloitte treats agent deployment as an enterprise architecture and control problem, not simply as chatbot implementation.

EY’s recent initiatives combine an industry transformation model with two large technology alliances. The EY–Microsoft initiative emphasizes embedded engineers, workforce adoption, secure industry agents and functions such as finance, tax, risk, HR and supply chain. The SymphonyAI expansion adds manufacturing intelligence and explicitly connects asset performance, materials planning, supplier collaboration and procurement execution. These initiatives indicate a preference for vertical value blueprints and alliance-enabled delivery rather than a single general-purpose EY-owned model.

PwC’s AI studio is an operating-model recommendation rather than a disclosed global implementation. It describes a centralized hub containing reusable components, use-case frameworks, a sandbox, deployment protocols and skilled people. The mechanism is important: senior leaders choose a small number of high-value workflows, while the studio industrializes experimentation and deployment. PwC’s own evidence also warns that many agentic deployments have produced little value when agents were attached to low-consequence or poorly redesigned workflows. [PwC’s 2026 AI predictions](https://www.pwc.com/us/en/tech-effect/ai-analytics/ai-predictions.html)

KPMG’s Workbench is more concrete as a named platform. Its architecture is deliberately multi-agent and multi-alliance, with data-sovereignty controls and a governance stamp. The combination with KPMG Clara, Digital Gateway and Velocity suggests a route into audit, tax and advisory workflows. KymChat provides a more localized Australian entry point, beginning with secure assistants and moving toward KPI-driven autonomous workers.

The MBB firms preserve a stronger distinction between strategic transformation and technology platforms than many systems integrators, but that distinction is narrowing. McKinsey’s QuantumBlack product suite includes deployable assets and multiple delivery models; BCG X structurally combines strategy and build; and Bain’s OpenAI alliance includes services, internal tools and enterprise deployment.

Their principal difference lies in how value is framed. McKinsey emphasizes “rewiring” the organization around six capabilities, BCG emphasizes the people-and-process component of transformation, and Bain emphasizes industry co-design and private-equity value creation. In practice, all three increasingly need engineering, data, change management and governance capabilities to convert strategy into production.

IBM’s distinctive initiative is not a single consulting methodology but a stack joining software, hybrid infrastructure, research and delivery assets. IBM Consulting Advantage makes the internal consulting process more repeatable, while watsonx supplies enterprise model, data and governance capabilities. IBM Sovereign Core extends that architecture to governments and regulated organizations that require control over identity, encryption, compliance evidence and AI execution.

Capgemini’s strategic change is more operational. WNS adds business-process scale, while the five value pools describe how Capgemini expects AI to reshape the technology debt, control plane, products, services and enterprise operations. Its Outcome Deployed Engineers model is intended to keep the firm accountable for deployed results rather than only strategy or prototypes, although the supplied disclosure does not report deployment counts or measured time-to-value.

The supplied evidence names Capgemini’s Resonance AI Framework and RAISE in a secondary comparison, but the retrieved primary page bodies do not expose enough detail to field them as fully documented products. The evidence therefore supports Capgemini’s WNS, AI value pools, delivery model, bookings and partner strategy more strongly than a complete named software catalog.

## 3. AI-driven products and services

The firms sell AI through six categories:

1. **Advisory:** strategy, maturity assessment, value prioritization, governance and operating-model design.
2. **Implementation:** data foundations, model integration, workflow redesign, agent development and deployment.
3. **Managed services:** ongoing operation of finance, tax, compliance, customer service, technology or business-process workflows.
4. **Software and platforms:** model development, assistants, orchestration, governance and data products.
5. **Industry solutions:** preconfigured agents, domain products and value blueprints.
6. **Internal productivity assets:** tools used by the firms’ own professionals, sometimes later packaged for clients.

A named internal tool is not automatically a commercial product. PairD, Sage and Lilli demonstrate internal adoption and delivery experience, but their reported internal usage should not be counted as external product revenue.

The Big Four catalog shows three distinct commercial positions. Deloitte offers an integrated decision and deployment layer, with Enterprise AI Navigator assessing where value and workflow change may occur before Zora or other agents are introduced. EY emphasizes enterprise and industry blueprints connected to audit, tax, manufacturing and Microsoft infrastructure. PwC emphasizes advisory, implementation and managed services organized around an AI studio and hybrid human-AI work. KPMG packages governed agents into platforms tied to audit, tax and advisory workflows.

The distinction matters for buyers. A maturity or roadmap service is not an agent platform; an agent platform is not a managed operation; and an internal assistant is not evidence of external deployment. The firms often place these categories under one brand, which makes the buyer’s task to identify exactly which component will be delivered, who will operate it and what metric defines success.

Accenture is the only firm in the supplied evidence with a branded platform explicitly organized around a large library of industry agents. Its proposition resembles a software product layered onto a global implementation and managed-services engine.

McKinsey’s product strategy is more domain-specific. Rather than presenting a single horizontal platform, QuantumBlack publishes a portfolio of industry products and offers three deployment models. This supports clients that want to retain infrastructure control as well as clients that want a managed service.

BCG X’s catalog is modular and industry-oriented. Data Intelligence AI, clean rooms and scenario-planning tools are designed to connect data preparation to business decisions. The product pages emphasize a reusable ecosystem but do not expose consistent dates, customer counts or outcome measures.

Bain’s commercial product layer is most visibly alliance-based. Sage is primarily an internal capability; the OpenAI Center of Excellence and Deployment Company are the client-facing mechanisms. The model is less about a Bain-owned horizontal platform than about combining frontier-model access with Bain’s industry, transformation and private-equity deployment expertise.

IBM Consulting Advantage then packages the firm’s consulting methods and knowledge into delivery assets.

Capgemini’s supported catalog is more service-oriented. WNS supplies operational scale, while the five value pools describe the architecture and business areas Capgemini intends to grow. The supplied evidence does not provide enough primary detail to treat “Perform AI,” Resonance or RAISE as fully fielded products with confirmed launch dates, customer counts and deployment outcomes. The safest description is that Capgemini has a strategic AI delivery model and named value pools, but a less completely disclosed product catalog than IBM, Accenture or KPMG.

## 4. AI outputs and measurable results

A common status ladder prevents announced capability from being confused with delivered value:

| Status | Meaning | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Announcement or target | A planned investment, product, rollout or future capability | Accenture’s more-than-100-agent target; Capgemini’s 2028 targets |
| Pipeline or development | Built or being developed, but not necessarily in production | KPMG’s nearly 1,000 assistants in development |
| Pilot or proof of concept | Tested in a bounded environment | IBM Consulting Advantage application-development pilot; Bain’s Bradesco call-center result |
| Live deployment | Used in production by a named client or workforce | KPMG footwear platform for more than 4,500 staff; CEMIG digital channels |
| Usage or adoption | A volume measure such as prompts, users, projects or customers | McKinsey’s 500,000-plus monthly prompts; Accenture’s 2,000-plus projects |
| Measured business outcome | A reported change in cost, time, revenue, productivity, quality or service | Bradesco’s 90% non-human resolution; BCG’s more-than-70% efficiency improvement at BEA |

### Accenture

Accenture said in January 2025 that it had supported more than 2,000 generative-AI projects across industries. The same announcement reported more than 600 marketing professionals equipped to use autonomous agents and access to more than 20 data sources. Content-production agents were still being piloted for broader deployment, so the 2,000-project figure represents supported work while the content-agent figure included both enabled users and a pipeline. [Accenture AI Refinery for Industry](https://newsroom.accenture.com/news/2025/accenture-launches-ai-refinery-for-industry-to-reinvent-processes-and-accelerate-agentic-ai-journeys)

A secondary benchmark attributes approximately 6,000 AI deployments, US$5.9 billion in AI bookings and approximately US$2.7 billion in GenAI and agentic-AI revenue to Accenture’s FY2025. Those figures are important because they suggest commercial scale beyond experimentation, but they are not defined in the supplied primary evidence with the same detail as Accenture’s 2,000-project disclosure. The benchmark also warns that bookings, revenue and deployment counts are not equivalent measures. [Consulting Huber comparison](https://consulting-huber.com/ai-consulting-frameworks-compared.html)

The Sanofi iCare+ deployment provides stronger client-scale evidence. Accenture says the platform was delivered in nine months, supported approximately 1,100 users from day one, laid the groundwork for launches in more than 20 markets, helped more than 650,000 patients and was onboarding more than 30,000 new patients per month. In the United States it handled more than 6,000 patient-service calls daily, with more than 35% of patients requiring patient-hub support enrolled in less than 30 days. These are reported operational measures, not a controlled causal evaluation. [Accenture Sanofi iCare+](https://www.accenture.com/gb-en/case-studies/life-sciences/sanofi-icare-patient-care)

### Deloitte

Deloitte’s strongest quantified evidence in the supplied material is a market survey rather than a firm delivery metric. Its 2026 State of AI in the Enterprise report, based on 3,235 leaders in 24 countries surveyed in August and September 2025, says 66% of organizations reported productivity and efficiency gains. It also distinguishes 34% beginning deep transformation, 30% redesigning key processes around AI and 37% using AI superficially. [Deloitte State of AI in the Enterprise](https://www.deloitte.com/us/en/what-we-do/capabilities/applied-artificial-intelligence/content/state-of-ai-in-the-enterprise.html)

The survey is useful for interpreting Deloitte’s service direction: it indicates that deployment is broad but deep transformation remains less common. It does not demonstrate that Deloitte’s own products caused those gains, nor does it provide a firm-specific revenue or deployment count.

Deloitte’s internal AI and learning outputs are more concrete. Its FY2025 announcement reports more than US$673 million of global Learning & Development investment and more than 21 million formal training hours for a workforce of more than 470,000. The AI Academy reports 30-plus hands-on courses and thousands of professionals reaching “100% AI fluency,” but the absolute number and completion period are not stated. [Deloitte AI Academy](https://www.deloitte.com/us/en/what-we-do/capabilities/applied-artificial-intelligence/about/deloitte-ai-academy.html)

### EY

EY reports that its internal “Client Zero” rollout initially deployed Copilot to 150,000 users and recorded a 15% productivity boost, with a planned expansion to more than 400,000 people worldwide. It also reports a finance-operation implementation with 95% faster lead times and a 37%-plus reduction in operational costs, and up to a 90% reduction in manual workload from Azure AI Document Intelligence on its Global Tax Platform. These are self-reported internal results; the announcement supplies no baseline, control group or independent evaluation. [EY–Microsoft initiative](https://www.ey.com/en_gl/newsroom/2026/05/ey-and-microsoft-announce-global-initiative-to-help-clients-scale-ai-enterprise-wide-value-creation-and-move-beyond-experimentation)

EY also reports that its multi-agent framework in EY Canvas covers the workflows of 130,000 Assurance professionals across 160,000 audit engagements. That is a workflow-reach measure, not a count of autonomous decisions or client outcomes. The distinction matters because access to an AI-enabled workflow does not establish active usage, quality improvement or financial return.

### PwC

PwC’s output evidence is strongest in named client cases and research. Its AI services page reports a Chipotle case in which agentic AI reduced time-to-fill by 75%, but does not identify the product, geography, date or baseline. A separate unnamed-pharmaceutical case reports a 20%–25% reduction in clinical-trial time and more than US$100 million in revenue increase, while leaving the cost reduction, precision improvement and baseline revenue unquantified. [PwC AI services](https://www.pwc.com/us/en/services/ai.html)

PwC’s 2025 Responsible AI survey found that 60% of respondents associated responsible AI with ROI and efficiency gains, while 55% associated it with better customer experience and innovation. Nearly half also said that operationalizing responsible-AI principles was challenging. This is evidence of perceived value and implementation difficulty, not a measurement of PwC’s own delivery output. [PwC AI predictions](https://www.pwc.com/us/en/tech-effect/ai-analytics/ai-predictions.html)

PwC’s 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer is a research output with unusually broad scale: more than one billion job advertisements across 27 countries and territories. It reports a 62% average wage premium for jobs requiring AI skills, AI-specific job growth of 69% compared with 9% for the overall jobs market, and 34% productivity growth in the most AI-exposed sectors versus 24% in the least able to use AI, measured in 2025 relative to 2018. These figures describe labor-market and company-level patterns, not PwC client deployments. [PwC 2026 AI Jobs Barometer](https://www.pwc.com/gx/en/news-room/press-releases/2026/pwc-2026-ai-jobs-barometer.html)

### KPMG

KPMG Workbench had a network of 50 assistants and chatbots at launch, with nearly 1,000 additional assistants in development. The first number is a platform inventory; the second is a development pipeline. KPMG also reported that clients were using Workbench for customer identity and fraud risk, telecommunications compliance and a multi-model digital workforce, but it did not provide quantified outcomes for those scenarios. [KPMG Workbench](https://kpmg.com/us/en/media/news/kpmg-launches-kpmg-workbench-a-multi-agent-ai-platform.html)

KPMG’s case evidence includes a live production platform for more than 4,500 corporate employees at a global footwear retailer. The case says KPMG continued to enhance and scale the platform after rollout and that user adoption and enablement were the client’s leading KPI, but it does not publish a numerical adoption rate. [KPMG footwear retailer case](https://kpmg.com/us/en/how-we-work/client-stories/unlocking-value-with-genai.html)

A transfer-pricing case reports 95% automation of documentation for a multinational company while retaining professional review, governance and approval. This is one of the clearest KPMG measured outcomes, but it is a single case and does not imply that all transfer-pricing work can be automated at the same level. [KPMG transfer-pricing case](https://kpmg.com/de/en/services/client-cases/95-per-cent-automation-100-per-cent-trust.html)

KPMG’s 2026 Global AI in Finance Report adds a market-level caution: active use of AI in finance more than doubled in two years, but only 23% of organizations said AI was exceeding expectations. That finding is consistent with KPMG’s governance-first positioning: adoption is growing faster than reliably demonstrated value. [KPMG Global AI in Finance Report](https://kpmg.com/xx/en/our-insights/ai-and-technology/kpmg-global-ai-in-finance-report.html)

### McKinsey

McKinsey reports 20-plus QuantumBlack products, more than 140 use cases, 200 R&D staff and collaboration with more than 1,000 industry and functional practitioners. It also reports that Lilli answered more than 500,000 prompts per month in September 2024. These figures establish product and internal-use scale but do not provide revenue or external deployment counts. [QuantumBlack product portfolio](https://www.mckinsey.com/about-us/new-at-mckinsey-blog/mckinseys-industry-ai-products-deliver-value-across-a-wide-range-of-use-cases) and [Lilli](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/mckinsey-digital/how-we-help-clients/rewiring-the-way-mckinsey-works-with-lilli)

McKinsey’s 2026 State of AI survey shows the gap between adoption and value. Forty percent of respondents from organizations with more than US$1 billion in annual revenue reported scaling AI agents, up from 27% the previous year; the corresponding share for smaller organizations was 22%. Yet only about 6% of all respondents qualified as AI high performers by attributing at least 5% of EBIT to AI and describing the impact as significant. [McKinsey State of AI](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/quantumblack/our-insights/the-state-of-ai)

This is not a contradiction. Agents can be scaling while value remains concentrated among a small group. McKinsey also reports that 80% of respondents saw individual productivity improvement and 50% reported better decisions, while 37% attributed at least some EBIT impact to AI. The results distinguish personal productivity and adoption from enterprise-level financial performance.

### BCG

BCG reports more than US$30 billion in value realized for clients from applied AI and more than 6,000 AI practitioners. Because the source does not state the measurement period, calculation basis or independent validation, these figures should be read as firm-reported scale indicators rather than an audited cumulative outcome. [BCG AI capabilities](https://www.bcg.com/capabilities/artificial-intelligence)

The BCG–Google Cloud partnership gives more concrete examples. Colgate-Palmolive’s Hill’s Pet Nutrition pilot produced consumer-ready video advertisements four to six times faster and at significantly lower cost per concept while achieving the same or better consideration lift than business as usual. At the Bank of East Asia, GenAI-powered SAS-code conversion and data-lineage work improved efficiency by more than 70%. The cost and consideration baselines are not fully disclosed. [BCG–Google Cloud partnership](https://www.bcg.com/press/22april2026-bcg-google-cloud-partnership-gemini-enterprise-transformation)

BCG’s 2026 AI Radar is a survey of client plans, not BCG expenditure. It reports that companies plan to double AI spending in 2026 to about 1.7% of revenue, and that 94% of CEOs intend to maintain or increase investment even if near-term returns are not achieved. More than 30% of planned AI investment is directed to agents. Those figures explain why consulting firms are expanding agentic offerings, but they do not measure BCG’s own investment. [BCG AI Radar 2026](https://www.bcg.com/press/15january2026-as-ai-investments-surge-ceos-take-lead)

### Bain

Bain reported that 12 internal AI tools had been rolled out since early 2023, including Sage, its proprietary GPT-4-based platform developed with OpenAI. The release reported no tool-level usage, revenue or external client-outcome measures. Bain also says it is recruiting engineers, data scientists and technology experts and providing training, but no hiring or training total is disclosed. [Bain AI tools](https://www.bain.com/about/media-center/press-releases/2023/bain--company-makes-pioneering-deployments-of-state-of-the-art-ai-tools-worldwide/)

Bain’s strongest measured outputs appear in client cases. Bradesco’s customer chatbot reached 90% retention against a 50% goal, resolved 90% of customer needs without human intervention and served millions of customers daily. A call-center chatbot reduced average handling time by 40% in a pilot. These are significant reported outcomes, but the retention metric and the pilot time reduction refer to different components of the broader program. [Bain Bradesco case](https://www.bain.com/client-results/ai/bradesco/)

### IBM

IBM’s headline generative-AI output is its more than US$12.5 billion book of business at the end of 2025. IBM defines this as inception-to-date software transactional revenue, new SaaS annual contract value and Consulting signings tied to specific offerings. It is therefore a combined booked-business measure, not AI-only recognized revenue, investment or deployment count. [IBM Q4 2025 results](https://newsroom.ibm.com/2026-01-28-IBM-RELEASES-FOURTH-QUARTER-RESULTS?hl=)

IBM Consulting Advantage produced up to a 50% productivity improvement in an early application design, development and testing client pilot, and IBM says it helped hundreds of clients apply AI in 2023. The percentage is a pilot result, and the release does not provide a baseline or independent validation. [IBM Consulting Advantage](https://stage.mediaroom.com/ibmnewsroom/2024-01-17-IBM-Introduces-IBM-Consulting-Advantage,-an-AI-Services-Platform-and-Library-of-Assistants-to-Empower-Consultants)

IBM also completed significant portfolio investments. HashiCorp was acquired for approximately US$7.2 billion in equity value, while IBM’s 2025 acquisitions in aggregate cost US$9.346 billion. IBM says these acquisitions advance hybrid cloud, automation, data and AI, but they cannot be reported as AI-only expenditure. [IBM 2025 Annual Report](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/51143/000005114326000010/ibm-20251231_d2.htm)

### Capgemini

Capgemini reports that GenAI bookings contributed more than 8% of Group bookings in FY2025 and more than 10% in the fourth quarter. Its CEO separately said generative and agentic AI accounted for more than 10% of Group bookings in Q4. These are bookings measures, not recognized revenue, deployed systems or client outcomes. [Capgemini FY2025 results](https://investors.capgemini.com/en/publication/fy-2025-results/)

Capgemini also reports €3.8 billion in 2025 acquisitions, WNS integration, 423,400 total employees at year-end and a strategic pivot toward AI-led transformation, Intelligent Operations and sovereignty. The WNS acquisition is directly connected to GenAI-powered intelligent operations, but neither WNS’s purchase price nor the AI share of the acquisition total is disclosed.

### What the output evidence shows

The evidence supports four judgments.

First, the market is moving from experiments toward production and operations, but not uniformly. Live deployments exist across all major groups, yet pipeline measures remain prominent.

Second, the most persuasive outcomes are workflow-specific. Bradesco’s resolution rate, BEA’s data-lineage efficiency, KPMG’s transfer-pricing automation and CEMIG’s digital-channel adoption describe a concrete process with a measurable endpoint. Broad claims such as “AI creates value” are less informative without a baseline, population and time period.

Third, bookings and book-of-business measures are commercially meaningful but should not be substituted for delivery. IBM’s US$12.5 billion and Capgemini’s bookings percentages show demand and commercial traction; they do not say how much work is complete or how much value clients have realized.

Fourth, self-reported outcomes need qualification. EY’s productivity and cost figures, BCG’s cumulative client-value estimate, IBM’s pilot productivity result and Accenture’s deployment counts are useful evidence, but the supplied material generally does not provide independent validation, control groups or full denominator definitions.

## 5. Client case studies and application scenarios

A useful case-study comparison asks four questions:

1. What business problem existed?
2. What AI intervention changed the process?
3. Which product, platform or service was used?
4. What outcome was delivered, and how strong is the evidence?

### Retail, customer service and marketing

| Firm and client | Geography, function and problem | AI intervention and product | Status and scale | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Accenture and Best Buy | Geography not stated; retail customer support faced troubleshooting, delivery and subscription-management demands | Accenture and Google built a virtual assistant across BestBuy.com, the app and phone support; care agents received real-time conversation analysis, guidance and sentiment tools | Live customer-support capability; thousands of care agents | Faster query resolution, more meaningful agent work and improved productivity and satisfaction are reported qualitatively; no quantified Best Buy outcome |
| Bain and Target | Geography not stated; store employees needed process support and new-member coaching; customers needed better product discovery | Store Companion chatbot; GenAI enhancements for hundreds of thousands of product-display pages; Bullseye Gift Finder | Launched use cases across stores, web, mobile and app | Qualitative benefits include more employee time with guests, more relevant product information and greater purchase confidence; no financial outcome reported |
| BCG, Google and Hill’s Pet Nutrition/Colgate-Palmolive | Client geography not stated; marketing content had to be produced at greater volume, variety and speed | GenAI content model producing consumer-ready video advertisements | Pilot, described in April 2026 partnership release | Ads produced four to six times faster, at significantly lower cost per concept, with same or better consideration lift; cost and lift differences not quantified |
| Accenture and Fortune | Geography not stated; business-intelligence content was difficult to use as an interactive product | Fortune Analytics LLM using Fortune rankings, articles and video transcripts, with on-demand charts | Delivered in ten months; product warns that generated information may be inaccurate or outdated | Improved user experience and potential new business model; no revenue or adoption metric reported |

The retail cases show that customer-facing AI is often less about open-ended conversation than about connecting a model to order systems, product information, subscription records and contact-center workflows. Best Buy’s assistant can change delivery or scheduling and manage subscriptions because it is integrated with operational systems; the language model is only one layer of the solution.

Target’s case shows a second pattern: the same client can apply GenAI to employee enablement, product-content production and recommendation. The shared mechanism is knowledge transformation—turning process information and catalog content into accessible, context-aware assistance. The case reports qualitative improvements but not sales, conversion or labor-hour effects.

BCG’s Hill’s Pet Nutrition case demonstrates why content-generation metrics need a quality comparator. Speed and cost alone could encourage low-quality output; the reported same-or-better consideration lift is therefore more meaningful than “four to six times faster” by itself. The limitation is that the release does not quantify either the cost reduction or the lift.

### Healthcare, life sciences and agriculture

| Firm and client | Geography, function and problem | AI intervention and product | Status and scale | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Accenture, Salesforce and Sanofi | Global specialty-therapy patient services; onboarding, insurance verification and fragmented provider interactions | iCare+ integrated Salesforce Health Cloud, Service Cloud, OCR, electronic benefit verification, real-time data, automation and agents | Delivered in nine months; more than 20 markets planned; around 1,100 users from day one | More than 650,000 patients helped; more than 30,000 new patients onboarding monthly; over 6,000 US calls daily; more than 35% of supported patients enrolled in under 30 days |
| PwC and unnamed leading pharmaceutical company | Geography and client name not stated; clinical trials are slow, costly and difficult to design | Data analytics and GenAI used to design a clinical trial and integrated technology platform with AWS and Microsoft | Delivered case described on PwC service page; date not stated | Time reduced by 20%–25% and revenue increased by more than US$100 million; cost and precision changes not quantified |
| McKinsey and Microsoft with unnamed top pharmaceutical company | Geography and client name not stated; market-access processes were manual, decentralized and data-siloed | Agentic-AI POCs, 14 core use cases, Microsoft Copilot for commercial-sales pre-call planning and an AI-enabled marketing-content platform | Phased 12–18-month deployment; POCs, six-month MVP and planned launch | Copilot associated with a 1%–2% revenue increase; content costs reduced 5%–20% and launch time reduced to 1–2 weeks |
| EY and Bayer/BCS | Client geography not stated; agronomic and product knowledge was difficult for advisors and farmers to retrieve | GenAI trained on agronomic and product knowledge through EY.ai | Knowledge-organization solution described; measured deployment scale not stated | Expected to help answer most agronomy and product questions faster and more completely; no measured speed, adoption or financial result |
| BCG and PHOENIX group | Global healthcare distribution and service operations; supply chains needed lower cost and better service | AI-enabled supply-chain transformation and workflow redesign | Client case; deployment date not stated | Improved service reported in 29 countries and employees freed for judgment-intensive work; absolute savings and measurement period not stated |

The healthcare cases reveal a critical difference between AI assistance and AI-enabled service transformation. Sanofi’s iCare+ involved data integration, insurance verification, service providers, specialty pharmacies, change management and market rollout. Its measured outputs are therefore operational—patients helped, calls handled and enrollment speed—rather than merely model-quality measures.

The pharmaceutical cases similarly combine agents with process redesign. McKinsey’s work did not begin with an enterprise-wide autonomous system; it began with a workshop, a use-case portfolio, POCs and a phased MVP. The reported revenue and content-cost results are stronger evidence than the plan itself, but the unnamed client limits external verification and generalization.

EY’s Bayer case remains an application example rather than a measured result. It establishes a plausible mechanism—organizing domain knowledge for faster retrieval—but the supplied source does not establish whether advisors used the tool, whether answer quality improved or whether farmer outcomes changed.

### Banking, finance, compliance and risk

| Firm and client | Geography, function and problem | AI intervention and product | Status and scale | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bain and Bradesco | Brazil; customer service and payments needed faster, more autonomous support | Customer-facing GenAI chatbot, call-center assistant and later agentic smart-payments pilot | Chatbot live and serving millions daily; payments features piloting in summer 2025 | 90% retention versus 50% goal; 90% of cases resolved without human intervention; call handling reduced 40% in pilot |
| BCG, Google Cloud and Bank of East Asia | Client geography not stated; SAS code conversion and data lineage were inefficient in a regulated setting | GenAI-powered data-management platform for code conversion and lineage extraction | Delivered client platform; date reported April 2026 | More than 70% improvement in code-conversion and lineage-extraction efficiency; no absolute cost or baseline |
| McKinsey and Emirates NBD | UAE; bank needed to scale advanced analytics with business adoption and governance | Lighthouse use cases embedded into business applications; federated governance, QuantumBlack CI/CD, feature store and validation framework | Transformation began in 2021; 70-plus analytics experts hired and trained in under two years | Talent and operating-model output reported; no aggregate revenue, cost or risk outcome in supplied case |
| KPMG and global bank | Geography not stated; identity verification, legitimacy and fraud risk required controlled data processing | Workbench agents with data sovereignty and multi-agent interaction | Client use reported at Workbench launch; quantified deployment and outcome not stated | Application and risk-mitigation objective reported; no measured result |
| KPMG and multinational company | Geography not stated; transfer-pricing documentation was complex and labor-intensive | AI structures data and prepares documentation within Trusted AI human-in-the-loop framework | Global implementation | 95% automation, higher quality and full control reported; professional review and approvals retained |
| IBM, Deloitte and regulated organizations | India and other regulated markets; data localization, security and compliance requirements | IBM Sovereign Core combined with Deloitte regulatory and transformation expertise | IBM Sovereign Core generally available May 2026; client outcomes not reported | Sovereign control, compliance evidence and in-boundary AI execution are capabilities, not measured client results |

Finance cases show why governance and architecture are not detachable from the business outcome. Bradesco’s chatbot reached high automation because it was embedded into customer channels and payment workflows. KPMG’s transfer-pricing case retained human approval because the cost of an opaque or incorrect tax document is materially different from the cost of an imperfect marketing draft.

Emirates NBD demonstrates a different scaling mechanism. The bank limited frontline change by embedding analytics outcomes into existing applications, while using central expertise and federated governance. The reported hiring and training of 70-plus experts is an organizational output; it does not, on its own, prove financial return.

### Industry, supply chain, energy and public-sector scenarios

|---|---|---|---|---|
| IBM and CEMIG | Brazil; energy provider had service-quality gaps across digital and traditional channels, especially in rural and underserved areas | watsonx.ai, Llama and Hugging Face models, NeuralSeek and integrated mobile, portal and WhatsApp channels | Client transformation described in 2025 case study; customer population described inconsistently as 9 million and more than 9.35 million across 774 municipalities | 82% of customers used digital channels for service requests; IBM cautions that results are illustrative and vary by configuration |
| Capgemini and BMDS | Germany; major infrastructure projects needed acceleration | Open-source and agent-based AI, according to the client-story title | Page title retrieved; body details unavailable | Client problem, product, date, scale and quantified outcome not retrieved |
| Capgemini and unnamed global conglomerate | Geography and client name not stated; supply-chain management improvement | Generative AI, according to the client-story title | Page title retrieved; body details unavailable | No quantified outcome, product, date or deployment scale retrieved |
| PwC Middle East flood-resilience tool | Middle East geography not specified; authorities and insurers need better flood-risk simulation | Geospatial AI using topography, rainfall, cyclones and ocean proximity, with dynamic 3D scenarios | Tool described as a solution; deployment scale not stated | Intended to support government agencies, emergency services, insurers and homeowners; no loss-reduction result reported |
| PwC Netherlands refugee model | Originally designed around Ukrainian refugees; authorities needed to assess interventions under unpredictable movements | AI model combining data, community research and expert knowledge across education, employment, sports and transport | Decision-support model; date and deployment scale not stated | Source says it outperforms human strategies but provides no numeric comparison |

| Deloitte and Olympic Movement | International sports; IOC and IPC needed an AI agenda and implementation direction | Olympic AI Agenda and technology-integration partnership | Agenda developed during Paris 2024; partnership from Milano Cortina 2026 onward | Strategic agenda and partnership reported; no AI deployment or outcome metric |

IBM’s CEMIG case demonstrates the value of combining open models, enterprise search and multiple service channels. The reported 82% digital-channel usage is a meaningful adoption measure, but the case itself warns that it is illustrative and that actual results vary. The inconsistent customer counts in the supplied page—9 million in the challenge description and more than 9.35 million later—also show why denominators must be preserved rather than silently harmonized.

Capgemini’s case evidence is currently the thinnest among the named firms. The titles establish that BMDS and a global conglomerate were associated with agent-based or generative AI in infrastructure and supply-chain work, but the retrieved bodies do not expose enough information to report a client problem, named product, delivery date or outcome. The correct conclusion is limited evidence, not an absence of delivery.

### Cross-case application map

| Application scenario | Sector and function | Modality or use case | Firm or product | Deployment maturity and outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Customer service and self-service | Retail, banking, energy; contact centers and digital channels | Conversational agents, retrieval, transaction execution and agent assistance | Accenture/Best Buy, Bain/Bradesco, IBM/CEMIG, KPMG Workbench | Live in named cases; measured results include Bradesco’s 90% non-human resolution and CEMIG’s 82% digital usage |
| Patient access and therapy support | Life sciences and healthcare; onboarding, coverage verification and patient services | Workflow agents, OCR, benefits verification, real-time data and automation | Accenture iCare+ | Live and scaled across markets; more than 650,000 patients helped and more than 30,000 monthly onboarding |
| Clinical research and market access | Pharmaceuticals; trial design, commercial sales and market access | GenAI analytics, POCs, Copilot and agentic workflows | PwC pharma case; McKinsey–Microsoft pharmaceutical case | Delivered or phased; reported 20%–25% time reduction, 1%–2% revenue increase and 5%–20% content-cost reduction |
| Marketing and content production | Consumer goods, retail and media | Generative text, video, product-page enhancement and personalization | BCG/Hill’s, Bain/Target, Accenture/Fortune | Pilot or live; four-to-six-times faster BCG content production, but several qualitative outcomes lack financial measures |
| Fraud, identity and compliance | Banking, telecom, tax and finance | Identity verification, fraud detection, controls and document automation | KPMG Workbench, KPMG transfer pricing, IBM watsonx | Live cases; 95% transfer-pricing automation; fraud and compliance outcomes not quantified |
| Supply chain and planning | Manufacturing, retail, energy and logistics | Forecasting, inventory, materials planning, supplier collaboration and asset intelligence | BCG Supply Chain AI, EY/SymphonyAI, Capgemini value pools, IBM Decision Optimization | Mix of product offering and announced solutions; measured client results limited to selected BCG cases |
| Software engineering and data modernization | Banking, pharma and enterprise IT | Code conversion, data lineage, application design and testing | BCG/BEA, IBM Consulting Advantage, McKinsey QuantumBlack | Live or pilot; BEA reports more than 70% efficiency improvement; IBM reports up to 50% pilot productivity |
| Knowledge and professional work | Consulting, audit, tax, agriculture and research | Enterprise retrieval, document extraction, domain knowledge access and decision support | McKinsey Lilli, EY Canvas and tax platform, EY/Bayer, Deloitte PairD | Internal or client deployments; usage and workload reductions reported, but quality and causal evidence vary |
| HR and workforce operations | Enterprise HR and talent functions | Employee-request agents, recruiting automation and workforce learning | IBM watsonx Orchestrate, PwC Chipotle case, Bain recruiting bot | Some live claims, some service examples; IBM reports 94% automated request resolution on its homepage, but methodology is not supplied |
| Sovereign and regulated AI | Government, finance, healthcare, defense and critical infrastructure | Local data control, in-boundary execution, multi-cloud/multi-model governance | Accenture Sovereign AI, IBM Sovereign Core, Deloitte Silicon2Service, KPMG Workbench | Strategic and platform maturity; client outcome evidence remains limited |

The cases show three recurring mechanisms.

**Integration beats isolated model access.** The strongest examples connect AI to CRM, ERP, claims, tax, patient-service, catalog or customer-channel systems. A model that cannot retrieve trusted data or execute an authorized workflow remains a demonstration.

**Human control is redesigned rather than simply removed.** KPMG’s tax case, McKinsey’s pharmaceutical deployment and BCG’s banking case all preserve human review or place AI inside a redesigned human-AI process. Automation is most credible when responsibility, exception handling and validation are explicit.

**The value metric depends on the workflow.** Resolution rate matters for customer service, enrollment speed for patient support, time-to-launch for content or marketing, code-lineage efficiency for data modernization and digital-channel adoption for utilities. A single cross-industry “AI ROI” number would hide these differences.

## 6. Strategic directions for AI

| Firm | Strategic priority | Target market and operating model | Industry focus | Responsible or sovereign position |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Accenture | Total-enterprise reinvention, industry agents and delivery at scale | Global strategy, consulting, technology, operations, Song and Industry X; platform plus ecosystem and managed delivery | Financial services, healthcare, retail, industrials, public sector, energy and sustainability | Sovereignty as a continuum; only about one-third of workloads need full sovereignty, with global and local providers combined |
| Deloitte | Agentic transformation with governance, value measurement and sovereign AI infrastructure | Navigator-led prioritization, Agentic Network, Zora and Silicon2Service; leadership-led governance | Customer support, supply chain, R&D, knowledge, cybersecurity, manufacturing, logistics and defense | Trustworthy AI, human-control boundaries, auditability, responsible design and sovereign AI factories |
| EY | Secure industry transformation and alliance-enabled enterprise adoption | EY.ai, Microsoft engineers, industry professionals, change management and value blueprints | Finance, tax, risk, HR, supply chain, manufacturing, energy, healthcare and consumer sectors | Secure, responsible and industry-specific agents; Microsoft and NVIDIA architecture; sovereignty emphasis is evidenced mainly through alliance and platform positioning |
| PwC | AI studio, hybrid human-AI work and managed services | Centralized reusable components and protocols linked to business-selected workflows | Finance, HR, IT, tax, internal audit, healthcare, retail, public sector and supply chain | Responsible AI through security, ethics, compliance, risk tiering and human intervention |
| KPMG | Governed multi-agent enterprise and recurring managed services | Workbench, KymX, Clara, Digital Gateway and Velocity; platform plus managed operation | Audit, tax, AML, corporate finance, finance operations and regulated sectors | Data sovereignty, ten-pillar Trusted AI, human-in-the-loop and ISO 42001 certification claim |
| McKinsey | Rewiring organizations around value, talent, technology and adoption | Strategy-led transformation with QuantumBlack products, managed deployment and operating-model redesign | Pharmaceuticals, healthcare, finance, insurance, retail, mining and enterprise software | Risk guardrails, security and resilience in products; explicit sovereign-AI position less prominent in supplied evidence |
| BCG | Value capture through workflow redesign, culture and human-AI collaboration | Deploy, Reshape and Invent; BCG X integrates strategy, product and engineering | Consumer, banking, industrial, supply chain, automotive, healthcare and life sciences | Governance and safety embedded in Google partnership; value emphasis exceeds explicit sovereignty positioning |
| Bain | OpenAI-led co-design and private-equity AI value creation | Alliance, Center of Excellence, Vector/Bain X and portfolio-company deployment | Retail, healthcare, life sciences, consumer, diligence and private-equity operations | Augmentation-oriented stance; responsible deployment is present in alliance language but less formally enumerated |
| IBM | Platform-centric hybrid-cloud AI and model choice | Software, consulting, infrastructure, research and alliances; open and hybrid deployment | Banking, healthcare, government, energy, technology and mission-critical operations | Strongest explicit sovereignty architecture through Sovereign Core; control, data residency and governed execution |
| Capgemini | Enterprise agentification, Intelligent Operations and sovereignty | Integrated strategy, technology, engineering, data and operations; WNS and Outcome Deployed Engineers | Manufacturing, financial services, public sector, energy, consumer, telecoms and technology | Sovereignty is a 2026 growth driver; primary material emphasizes partner-enabled and European-scale delivery |

### Accenture: scale, reinvention and a sovereignty continuum

Accenture’s strategic model combines a large workforce, industry assets, platform engineering, hyperscaler alliances and operations delivery. Its AI Refinery for Industry is designed to convert the general capability of foundation models into reusable industry agents. This is a scale strategy: reduce the time and cost of building agents, reuse patterns across sectors and move from consulting design into implementation and operations.

Its sovereignty position is more flexible than a full localization model. Accenture defines sovereign AI as the ability to develop and deploy AI using controlled infrastructure, data, models and talent, but argues that only one-third of an organization’s workloads need to be sovereign. The recommendation is to combine global and local providers according to use-case risk, regulation and value. Its 2025 survey of 1,928 leaders across 28 countries found that only 15% had made sovereignty a CEO or board-level concern, while data sovereignty and infrastructure controls were more common than model or application controls. [Accenture Sovereign AI report](https://www.accenture.com/content/dam/accenture/final/accenture-com/document-4/Sovereign-AI-Report.pdf)

The operating implication is a mixed architecture: global models and cloud where scale and innovation matter, regional providers and local data controls where regulation, resilience or national capability matter. Accenture’s examples in Indonesia, Canada and Sweden show how the firm tries to act as ecosystem orchestrator rather than insisting on one proprietary stack.

### Big Four: governance becomes a growth product

The Big Four firms have a structural advantage in governance because audit, risk, compliance and regulated-industry work are already central to their businesses. Their AI strategies increasingly turn that advantage into products and managed services.

Deloitte’s research argues that senior leadership involvement in AI governance is associated with greater business value than delegating governance only to technical teams. It recommends defined human-control boundaries, audited automated decisions, retained system records, high-risk-use identification and independent validation. The strategic direction is therefore not “govern first and deploy later,” but “governance as a condition for scaling agents.” [Deloitte State of AI in the Enterprise](https://www.deloitte.com/us/en/what-we-do/capabilities/applied-artificial-intelligence/content/state-of-ai-in-the-enterprise.html)

EY positions itself around enterprise-wide, industry-specific AI that intersects with finance, tax, assurance, risk, HR and supply chain. Its Microsoft alliance emphasizes forward-deployed engineers and change management, while the SymphonyAI expansion adds manufacturing intelligence. The operating model is alliance-enabled and blueprint-driven: identify a high-value industry process, combine EY domain professionals with technology specialists and embed adoption support.

PwC’s strategy is more explicitly organized around the AI studio and hybrid human-AI teams. It argues that agentic AI changes who performs work, so organizations must redesign value chains, workflows, roles and skills. Its responsible-AI evidence is deliberately ambivalent: respondents see ROI and customer benefits, but nearly half struggle to operationalize responsible-AI principles. That tension supports PwC’s emphasis on repeatable governance and managed services rather than one-off pilots.

KPMG places governance at the center of the platform itself. Workbench agents carry a Trusted AI stamp, data sovereignty is built into the platform, and KPMG connects the platform to audit, tax and advisory products. Its strategic model is especially suited to organizations that need evidence of controls, model risk management and human approval. The limitation is that a governance framework does not itself prove business value; KPMG’s own finance survey shows that only 23% of organizations report AI exceeding expectations.

### McKinsey, BCG and Bain: from strategy to applied transformation

McKinsey’s Rewired approach treats AI as an organizational capability rather than a technology installation. Its six capabilities—value-linked transformation roadmaps, talent, operating model, technology environment, data and adoption—explain why the firm combines strategy work with QuantumBlack products and deployment models. The 2026 State of AI findings reinforce the premise: usage and agent scaling are rising, while only a small share of organizations report significant EBIT impact.

BCG’s 10-20-70 logic puts even more emphasis on work design. Its synthesis attributes only 10% of transformation value to the AI application, 20% to data and technology, and 70% to workflow redesign, culture, governance and human-AI collaboration. BCG’s Deploy, Reshape and Invent structure moves from productivity use cases to process redesign and new products. This is a strategic position about where value is captured, not a claim that every engagement follows a fixed mathematical formula. [BCG AI capabilities](https://www.bcg.com/capabilities/artificial-intelligence)

Bain’s direction is more alliance- and transaction-oriented. OpenAI supplies frontier-model access, while Bain contributes industry strategy, transformation and private-equity value-creation capability. The Deployment Company investment extends that logic to portfolio companies, with applications spanning product development, customer experience, automation, cost and supply chain. Bain’s stated view that AI augments rather than replaces consultants also shapes its talent strategy: recruit technical specialists into consulting teams and use AI to increase the reach of human judgment.

### IBM: hybrid cloud, model choice and sovereign control

IBM’s annual report describes a platform-centric hybrid-cloud and AI strategy combining software, consulting, industry expertise, infrastructure, trust and research. Its model is different from a pure advisory firm because IBM can supply the model-development platform, data layer, governance tools, infrastructure and consulting operation.

The platform is intentionally hybrid and model-flexible. IBM says clients need to infer, govern and manage multiple models, data flows and applications across environments. Its open models, watsonx stack, Red Hat platforms and partner ecosystem are designed to let clients choose where and how workloads run. [IBM 2025 Annual Report](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/51143/000005114326000010/ibm-20251231_d2.htm)

Sovereignty is the clearest strategic extension of this model. IBM Sovereign Core gives enterprises and governments a software architecture for customer-operated control, in-boundary identity, encryption, compliance evidence and governed AI execution. Deloitte’s partnership around India’s data-localization and DPDP requirements illustrates how IBM combines platform control with external regulatory expertise.

### Capgemini: agentification, intelligent operations and sovereignty

Capgemini’s strategy is to move AI from experiments into the full enterprise value chain. Its five value pools cover legacy modernization, the agentic stack, the control plane, products and services, and enterprise operations. WNS strengthens the final category by adding business-process delivery at scale.

This is a delivery-led model. Capgemini combines strategy, technology, data and AI, engineering and operations through Outcome Deployed Engineers and AI-native delivery setups. The objective is to shorten time-to-value, but the May 2026 announcement does not provide a measured time-to-value result.

Capgemini also identifies sovereignty as a growth driver, alongside Intelligent Operations and AI-led transformation programs. Its geography and European heritage make data localization, regulatory requirements and public-sector trust commercially relevant, while its alliance ecosystem supplies cloud and infrastructure scale. The central strategic risk is execution: the value-pool framework is broad, and the supplied evidence does not yet provide a uniform set of product-level deployments and outcomes.

## 7. AI talent development programs

Talent programs differ in audience and evidence strength. Some train the firms’ own professionals; some train clients; some recruit technical specialists; and some are national workforce commitments. A participant target is not a completion result, and access to a platform is not the same as demonstrated proficiency.

| Program or initiative | Firm | Audience and format | Skills covered and scale | Status and reported outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Generative AI Scholars Program | Accenture | Business and technology leaders; more than 40 hours of self-paced online learning combining Stanford Online content and Accenture instruction | Foundation models, prompt engineering, agentic architecture, human-centered and responsible AI; intended reach of thousands; certificate on completion | Launched December 2024; intended reach, not completed participant total |
| Foundation Models Scholar Program | Accenture | Executives and senior leaders; three-day in-person intensive | Generative-AI use cases and industry applications | About 150 leaders reached in the 2022 predecessor program |
| AI Academy | Deloitte | Professionals at all experience levels; 30-plus hands-on courses | AI, GenAI, agentic AI, emerging technologies and Deloitte tools | Thousands reported at 100% AI fluency; absolute number and completion period not stated |
| Global Learning & Development | Deloitte | More than 470,000 people; formal learning and technology reskilling | GenAI, agentic AI, cloud and cybersecurity among broader learning | More than US$673 million direct investment and more than 21 million formal training hours in FY2025 |
| NextGen Tech Academy | Deloitte Ireland | Technical and non-technical applicants in Dublin; paid 12-month contract with 12-week accelerated training | Cloud, infrastructure as code, CI/CD, DevOps, AI applications, ML, predictive analytics and automation | Program structure reported; participant target and post-program outcome not stated |
| AI Academy India | EY | Employees and enterprise participants; role-specific, hands-on and project-based tracks | Four tracks: leadership manifesto, transformation champions, broad fundamentals and deep technical implementation | Launched July 2025; more than 44,000 EY India employees already upskilled; 200-plus use cases |
| EY enterprise pilot and Techathon | EY | Enterprise leaders and college students | Leadership AI manifestos, sector use cases and student problem-solving | Pilot across five enterprises initiated more than 50 AI projects; student participation total not stated |
| PwC GenAI upskilling and ChatPwC rollout | PwC | PwC professionals; secondary evidence reports US and international users | GenAI use, tax and professional knowledge; 65,000 US employees reportedly upskilled and approximately 200,000 users given ChatPwC access | Figures come from a secondary comparison; primary program details and completion results not retrieved |
| KymChat training and Workbench enablement | KPMG | Client employees and KPMG professionals | Secure assistants, prompt and workflow use, governance and agent adoption | KymChat says many clients see initial value within weeks; participant and completion totals not stated |
| AI capability development | McKinsey | Firm professionals and client teams | QuantumBlack, analytics, product deployment and AI operating models | Firm-wide training totals not retrieved; Emirates NBD client case reports 70-plus analytics experts hired and trained |
| AI practitioners and client literacy | BCG | BCG practitioners and client workforces | AI delivery, transformation and AI fluency | BCG reports 6,000-plus AI practitioners; one unnamed client reportedly moved from 18% to 90% AI literacy |
| Technical recruiting and internal training | Bain | Consultants, engineers, data scientists and technology specialists | AI tools, technical curiosity, applied delivery and employee productivity | Bain says it is hiring more technical specialists and training employees; no hiring or completion target stated |
| IBM SkillsBuild AI learning pathway | IBM | UK workforce from entry-level employees to senior leaders and policymakers; free progressive online pathway | LLMs, prompt engineering, ethics, data analytics, fraud, risk, ML, NLP, solution development and governance; Level 6 leadership and policy module | Announced June 2026; UK AI Skills Boost aims to upskill 10 million workers by 2030; this is a target, not a completed total |
| IBM watsonx certification | IBM | Technical learners; certification listing | “IBM Certified watsonx Generative AI Engineer – Associate” | Certification exists, but audience, date, participant total and outcome are not stated in the supplied listing |
| AI-related learning and workforce adaptation | Capgemini | Global employees; country-specific reskilling and skills-adaptation initiatives | Broad learning with particular focus on AI-related upskilling | Average learning reached 97 hours per employee in 2025 versus a 70-hour objective; approximately €700 million restructuring costs anticipated over two years |
| Capgemini Data & AI Campus | Capgemini | Employees; secondary evidence reports GenAI-tool upskilling | Generative-AI tools and data/AI capabilities | A secondary comparison reports more than 150,000 people upskilled; primary confirmation and completion details not retrieved |

### Accenture and Deloitte: structured internal fluency

Accenture’s programs move from executive immersion to scalable self-paced learning. The earlier Foundation Models Scholar Program reached about 150 leaders through a three-day intensive in 2022. The 2024 Generative AI Scholars Program expands accessibility and adds a certificate, agentic architecture and responsible AI. The design reflects a two-level problem: senior leaders need strategic fluency, while wider technical and business populations need practical skill.

Deloitte combines formal corporate learning investment with a dedicated AI Academy. The reported US$673 million and 21 million training hours include learning beyond AI, so they should not be counted as AI-only spending. The AI Academy’s 30-plus courses and thousands of professionals reaching full fluency show a more focused internal curriculum, but the missing absolute participant count limits comparison.

Deloitte Ireland’s NextGen Academy is a pipeline program rather than a mass online rollout. Its paid 12-month structure, six-week immersive technical phase, client projects and mentorship connect training directly to delivery. The absence of a participant target or placement outcome means it demonstrates program design rather than program scale.

### EY: role-based and enterprise-linked learning

EY India’s AI Academy is the most completely described role-based program in the supplied evidence. Its four tracks distinguish leadership, transformation execution, broad AI literacy and deep technical implementation. The use of more than 200 real-world cases is intended to move learning from abstract prompting to sector-specific use-case execution.

The reported 44,000-plus internal upskilling result is a completed workforce measure, while the five-enterprise pilot and more than 50 initiated AI projects show an enterprise-facing output. They should not be conflated: the first measures EY employees, the second measures client projects initiated through a pilot.

The global EY–Microsoft initiative adds another layer by embedding engineers, industry professionals, change management and workforce upskilling into client deployments. No participant target or completed client-training total is reported.

### PwC, KPMG and the MBB firms: capability without uniform totals

PwC’s secondary-reported 65,000 US upskilled employees and approximately 200,000 ChatPwC users suggest very large internal diffusion, but the supplied primary pages do not expose a consistent program description, certification format or completion result. PwC’s Global AI Jobs Barometer provides the external labor-market context: AI skills command a 62% wage premium, and companies most exposed to AI are hiring faster than less exposed firms. That evidence supports investment in reskilling but does not fill the missing PwC program fields.

KPMG emphasizes enablement alongside governed tools. Workbench and KymChat provide training and rollout support, while the platform’s Trusted AI stamp formalizes the skills required to use agents safely. However, KPMG does not report a global participant total, certification volume or completed reskilling result in the supplied material.

McKinsey’s firm-wide training total is unavailable. The Emirates NBD case is a client workforce program: more than 70 analytics experts were hired and trained in less than two years, supported by a federated operating model. It should not be presented as McKinsey’s own talent output.

BCG reports 6,000-plus AI practitioners and a client AI-literacy example moving from 18% to 90%, but it does not name a firm-wide curriculum, participant target or certification format. BCG’s AI Radar reports that companies led by “Trailblazing” CEOs allocate 60% of their AI budgets to upskilling and retraining, compared with 27% for Pragmatists and 24% for Followers. That is a client survey archetype, not a BCG training program. [BCG AI Radar 2026](https://www.bcg.com/press/15january2026-as-ai-investments-surge-ceos-take-lead)

Bain’s talent direction is clearer than its scale. The firm says it is hiring engineers, data scientists and technology experts to work alongside consultants, widening recruitment beyond the traditional campus footprint. It provides training for internal GenAI deployment and is developing Reggie the Recruiter, but no hiring volume, participant total or measured training result is reported. [Bain’s AI-era recruiting discussion](https://www.bain.com/insights/How-is-AI-Changing-the-Way-Bain-Hires-Consultants/)

### IBM and Capgemini: national scale and reskilling economics

IBM SkillsBuild provides the most explicit public workforce-scale commitment: the UK AI Skills Boost partnership aims to upskill 10 million UK workers by 2030. The pathway is progressive, moving from LLMs and prompting to machine learning, NLP, solution development and leadership. The Level 6 module recognizes that executives and policymakers need governance and transformation skills, not only technical skills. The 10 million figure is an ambition, not a completed participant total. [IBM SkillsBuild pathway](https://uk.newsroom.ibm.com/ibm-launches-new-ai-learning-pathway)

IBM’s annual report also describes skill-based hiring, advanced learning and reskilling across a workforce of approximately 264,300 IBM employees and complementary workers. It does not provide an AI-certification total or a firm-wide completion rate. IBM’s product certification listing confirms an associate-level watsonx credential, but the supplied page does not provide enrollment or outcome data.

Capgemini reports 97 average learning hours per employee in 2025, well above its objective of maintaining 70 hours. The result is a broad learning measure with an AI focus, not a count of certified AI specialists. Capgemini also anticipates approximately €700 million of restructuring costs over two years, largely in 2026, to adapt workforce skills to AI-driven demand. This is a forward-looking workforce investment and cost, not a completed reskilling output.

The talent evidence points to a common transition: firms are moving from generic awareness toward role-specific adoption, technical engineering, leadership governance and process redesign. The most important missing metric across the market is not course volume but demonstrated transfer: how many trained people deploy AI safely in live workflows, and how much of the capability remains with the client after the consulting engagement.
